cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which view explains why a generally aggressive person may act submissively before her/his top boss?
cards.back:
Situationism
A person, who is generally aggressive, may behave in a submissive manner in the presence of her/his top boss.
cards.quote: A person, who is generally aggressive, may behave in a submissive manner in the presence of her/his top boss.
reasons: review:Illustrative case-story; situationism definition card already carries the mark-bearing content

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name Gardner's eight types of intelligence.
cards.back:
Linguistic (an ability to produce and use language)
Logical-Mathematical (an ability to think logically and critically, and solve problems)
Spatial (an ability to form visual images and patterns)
Musical (an ability to produce and manipulate musical rhythms and patterns)
Bodily-Kinaesthetic (an ability to use whole or portions of the body flexibly and creatively)
Interpersonal (an ability to understand to subtle aspects of others' behaviours)
Intrapersonal (an ability to understand of one's own feelings, motives, and desires)
Naturalistic (an ability to identify the features of the natural world)
cards.quote: Gardner studied extremely talented persons, who had shown exceptional abilities in their respective areas, and described eight types of intelligence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the three components of componential intelligence.
cards.back:
knowledge acquisition component, which is responsible for learning and acquisition of the ways of doing things
meta or a higher order component, which involves planning concerning what to do and how to do
performance component, which involves actually doing things
cards.quote: This intelligence has three components, each serving a different function.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: These units are responsible for ____, coding or processing, and planning respectively.
cards.back: These units are responsible for arousal/attention, coding or processing, and planning respectively.
cards.quote: These units are responsible for arousal/attention, coding or processing, and planning respectively.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the intelligence correlations reported for twins and siblings.
cards.back:
identical twins reared in different environments correlate 0.72
fraternal twins reared together correlate almost 0.60
brothers and sisters reared together correlate about 0.50
siblings reared apart correlate about 0.25
cards.quote: The intelligence of identical twins reared in different environments correlate 0.72, those of fraternal twins reared together correlate almost 0.60, and those of brothers and sisters reared together correlate about 0.50, while siblings reared apart correlate about 0.25.

source.section: Intelligence: Interplay of Nature and Nurture

reasons: review:Back omits the first reported correlation (identical twins reared together, almost 0.90) though front asks for the correlations; incomplete list, exact back is partial

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Formula: IQ.
cards.back: IQ refers to mental age divided by chronological age, and multiplied by 100.
cards.quote: IQ refers to mental age divided by chronological age, and multiplied by 100.
reasons: review:Formula card does not show the formula NCERT prints (IQ = MA/CA x 100); back is the prose sentence already on the def-iq-stern card (duplicate content)

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Those with IQ below ____ are suspected to have "intellectual disability", while persons with IQ above ____ are considered to have exceptional talents.
cards.back: Those with IQ below 70 are suspected to have "intellectual disability", while persons with IQ above 130 are considered to have exceptional talents.
cards.quote: Those with IQ below 70 are suspected to have "intellectual disability", while persons with IQ above 130 are considered to have exceptional talents.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Classify people on the basis of IQ range (Table 1.1), highest to lowest.
cards.back:
Above 130 Very superior
120 – 130 Superior
110 – 119 High average
90 – 109 Average
80 – 89 Low average
70 – 79 Borderline
Below 70 Intellectually disabled
cards.quote: The IQ score of a person can be interpreted by referring to Table 1.1.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the three basic features of intellectual disability (AAMD definition).
cards.back:
significantly sub-average intellectual functioning
deficits in adaptive behaviour
the deficits must be observed during the developmental period, that is between 0 and 18 years of age
cards.quote: This definition points to three basic features.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The highly talented are sometimes called "____".
cards.back: The highly talented are sometimes called "prodigies".
cards.quote: The highly talented are sometimes called "prodigies".

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the early signs of intellectual superiority shown by gifted children.
cards.back:
larger attention span
good recognition memory
preference for novelty
sensitivity to environmental changes
early appearance of language skills
cards.quote: Gifted children show early signs of intellectual superiority.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the important characteristics of gifted children.
cards.back:
Advanced logical thinking, questioning and problem solving behaviour.
High speed in processing information.
Superior generalisation and discrimination ability.
Advanced level of original and creative thinking.
High level of intrinsic motivation and self-esteem.
Independent and non-conformist thinking.
Preference for solitary academic activities for long periods.
cards.quote: Some important characteristics of gifted children are :

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the ill-effects of intelligence testing by naive testers.
cards.back:
Poor performance on a test may attach a stigma to children and thereby adversely affect their performance and self-respect.
The tests may invite discriminating practices from parents, teachers and elders in the society.
Administering a test biased in favour of the middle class and higher class populations may underestimate the IQ of children coming from disadvantaged sections of the society.
Intelligence tests do not capture creative potentialities and practical side of intelligence, and they also do not relate much to success in life.
cards.quote: Some of the ill-effects of intelligence testing by naive testers are:

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which Indian test is quite popular among those listed in Table 1.2?
cards.back: Among these, Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests is quite popular.
cards.quote: Among these, Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests is quite popular.
reasons: review:Front depends on Table 1.2 (not shown) and several Indian tests exist, so answer not derivable from front; Indian test names are low-yield trivia

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the facets of intelligence in the Indian tradition.
cards.back:
Cognitive capacity (sensitivity to context, understanding, discrimination, problem solving, and effective communication).
Social competence (respect for social order, commitment to elders, the young and the needy, concern about others, recognising others' perspectives).
Emotional competence (self-regulation and self-monitoring of emotions, honesty, politeness, good conduct, and self-evaluation).
Entrepreneurial competence (commitment, persistence, patience, hard work, vigilance, and goal-directed behaviours).
cards.quote: Unlike the western views, which primarily focus on cognitive parameters, the following competencies are identified as facets of intelligence in the Indian tradition :

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Characteristics of emotionally intelligent persons (Box 1.2).
cards.back:
Perceive and be sensitive to your feelings and emotions.
Perceive and be sensitive to various types of emotions in others by noting their body language, voice and tone, and facial expressions.
Relate your emotions to your thoughts so that you take them into account while solving problems and taking decisions.
Understand the powerful influence of the nature and intensity of your emotions.
Control and regulate your emotions and their expressions while dealing with self and others to achieve harmony and peace.
cards.quote: Characteristics of Emotionally Intelligent Persons

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define aptitude as a special ability.
cards.back: Aptitude refers to special abilities in a particular field of activity. It is a combination of characteristics that indicates an individual's capacity to acquire some specific knowledge or skill after training.
cards.quote: Aptitude refers to special abilities in a particular field of activity. It is a combination of characteristics that indicates an individual's capacity to acquire some specific knowledge or skill after training.
reasons: review:Ambiguous with def-aptitude-attribute (two different NCERT aptitude definitions, fronts differ only by 'as a ...'); also Key Term so should be must

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Hence, a certain level of intelligence is required for creativity but beyond that intelligence does not ____ well with creativity.
cards.back: Hence, a certain level of intelligence is required for creativity but beyond that intelligence does not correlate well with creativity.
cards.quote: Hence, a certain level of intelligence is required for creativity but beyond that intelligence does not correlate well with creativity.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the psychologists who have developed creativity tests.
cards.back:

Torrance
Khatena

Paramesh

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does the term "intelligence" refer to (chapter summary)?
cards.back: The term "intelligence" refers to an individual's capacity to understand the world, think rationally, and use resources effectively to meet the demands of life.
cards.quote: The term "intelligence" refers to an individual's capacity to understand the world, think rationally, and use resources effectively to meet the demands of life.
reasons: review:Duplicate of def-intelligence-attribute: two valid NCERT definitions answer 'What is intelligence?'; student cannot tell which is wanted

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does emotional intelligence involve (chapter summary)?
cards.back: Emotional intelligence involves the ability to perceive and manage one's and other's feelings and emotions; to motivate oneself and restrain one's impulses; and to handle interpersonal relationships effectively.
cards.quote: Emotional intelligence involves the ability to perceive and manage one's and other's feelings and emotions; to motivate oneself and restrain one's impulses; and to handle interpersonal relationships effectively.
reasons: review:Overlaps def-emotional-intelligence: two valid NCERT answers to 'what is emotional intelligence/what does it involve'; front cannot pick one

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: A strong sense of ____ allows people to select, influence, and even construct the circumstances of their own life.
cards.back: A strong sense of self-efficacy allows people to select, influence, and even construct the circumstances of their own life.
cards.quote: A strong sense of self-efficacy allows people to select, influence, and even construct the circumstances of their own life.
reasons: review:Blank has no unique fill from the line; self-esteem or self-confidence also fit

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The ____ approach holds that situational characteristics play an important role in determining our behaviour.
cards.back: The interactional approach holds that situational characteristics play an important role in determining our behaviour.
cards.quote: The interactional approach holds that situational characteristics play an important role in determining our behaviour.

source.section: Major Approaches to the Study of Personality

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Each refers to a type of temperament, called ____ (basic nature) of a person.
cards.back: Each refers to a type of temperament, called prakriti (basic nature) of a person.
cards.quote: Each refers to a type of temperament, called prakriti (basic nature) of a person.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which qualities do Birhor child socialisation practices aim at?
cards.back: Their child socialisation practices are also aimed at making children independent (do many things without help from elders), autonomous (take several decisions for themselves), and achievement-oriented (accept risks and challenges such as those involved in hunting) from an early age of life.
cards.quote: Their child socialisation practices are also aimed at making children independent (do many things without help from elders), autonomous (take several decisions for themselves), and achievement-oriented (accept risks and challenges such as those involved in hunting) from an early age of life.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Who developed the Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire (16 PF), and how did he identify the basic personality structure?
cards.back: This test was developed by Cattell. On the basis of his studies, he identified a large set of personality descriptors, which were subjected to factor analysis to identify the basic personality structure.
cards.quote: This test was developed by Cattell. On the basis of his studies, he identified a large set of personality descriptors, which were subjected to factor analysis to identify the basic personality structure.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Draw-a-Person Test: name the examples of interpretations given.
cards.back:
Omission of facial features suggests that the person tries to evade a highly conflict-ridden interpersonal relationship.
Graphic emphasis on the neck suggests lack of control over impulses.
Disproportionately large head suggests organic brain disease and preoccupation with headaches.
cards.quote: (1) Omission of facial features suggests that the person tries to evade a highly conflict-ridden interpersonal relationship. (2) Graphic emphasis on the neck suggests lack of control over impulses. (3) Disproportionately large head suggests organic brain disease and preoccupation with headaches.
reasons: review:Illustrative interpretation examples (neck, head, facial features) are case filler, not exam-tested

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the different kinds of self.
cards.back:
personal self
social self
relational self

reasons: review:'Different kinds of self' also fits subject/object self and real/ideal self; also overlaps social vs relational self in card def-social-self

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Stress is like ____. It gives energy, increases human ____ and affects performance.
cards.back: Stress is like electricity. It gives energy, increases human arousal and affects performance.
cards.quote: Stress is like electricity. It gives energy, increases human arousal and affects performance.

cards.quote: The more stress people report as a result of daily hassles, the poorer is their psychological well-being.

cards.front: This state of physical, emotional and psychological exhaustion is known as ____.
cards.back: This state of physical, emotional and psychological exhaustion is known as burnout.
cards.quote: This state of physical, emotional and psychological exhaustion is known as burnout.
cards.note: Burnout follows physical exhaustion (chronic fatigue, weakness) and mental exhaustion (irritability, helplessness).

cards.back: It is these T-helper cells that are attacked by the Human Immuno Deficiency Virus (HIV)

cards.front: What is lifestyle?
cards.back: Lifestyle is the overall pattern of decisions and behaviours that determine a person's health and quality of life.
cards.quote: Lifestyle is the overall pattern of decisions and behaviours that determine a person's health and quality of life.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: it is how we ____ with stress and not the stress one experiences that influences our psychological well-being, social functioning and health.
cards.back: it is how we cope with stress and not the stress one experiences that influences our psychological well-being, social functioning and health.
cards.quote: it is how we cope with stress and not the stress one experiences that influences our psychological well-being, social functioning and health.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Avoidance-oriented coping strategy (Endler and Parker).
cards.back: This involves denying or minimising the seriousness of the situation; it also involves conscious suppression of stressful thoughts
cards.quote: Avoidance-oriented Strategy : This involves denying or minimising the seriousness of the situation; it also involves conscious suppression of stressful thoughts
reasons: review:Endler and Parker avoidance-oriented strategy parallels task-oriented (must); should be must; quote and back are cut mid-sentence; NCERT continues "and their replacement by self-protective thoughts"

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which type of coping is this? “I made a plan of action and followed it”.
cards.back: They can act to reduce the threat value of the event. For example “I made a plan of action and followed it”.
cards.quote: They can act to reduce the threat value of the event. For example “I made a plan of action and followed it”.
reasons: review:back does not state the answer (problem-focused) and opens with dangling "They"; example card must name the concept; "I made a plan of action and followed it" fits both problem-focused and task-oriented coping

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which type of coping is this? “I did some things to let it out of my system”.
cards.back: Emotion-focused strategies call for psychological changes designed primarily to limit the degree of emotional disruption caused by an event, with minimal effort to alter the event itself. For example “I did some things to let it out of my system”.
cards.quote: Emotion-focused strategies call for psychological changes designed primarily to limit the degree of emotional disruption caused by an event, with minimal effort to alter the event itself. For example “I did some things to let it out of my system”.
reasons: review:"let it out of my system" fits both emotion-focused (Lazarus) and emotion-oriented (Endler and Parker); back repeats definition rather than naming concept alone

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Usually relaxation starts from the ____ part of the body and progresses up to the ____ muscles in such a way that the whole body is relaxed.
cards.back: Usually relaxation starts from the lower part of the body and progresses up to the facial muscles in such a way that the whole body is relaxed.
cards.quote: Usually relaxation starts from the lower part of the body and progresses up to the facial muscles in such a way that the whole body is relaxed.
reasons: review:blank "lower" has rival fills (bottom, lowest); low-value procedural detail

cards.subject: psychology

cards.quote: Before visualising one must set oneself a realistic goal, as it helps build confidence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Whereas stretching exercises have a ____ effect, ____ exercises increase the arousal level of the body.
cards.back: Whereas stretching exercises have a calming effect, aerobic exercises increase the arousal level of the body.
cards.quote: Whereas stretching exercises have a calming effect, aerobic exercises increase the arousal level of the body.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is informational social support?
cards.back: Family and friends also provide informational support about stressful events.
cards.quote: Family and friends also provide informational support about stressful events.
reasons: review:circular sentence ("provide informational support"), no real definition or example; better as one list card of tangible/informational/emotional support

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Stress is neither a stimulus nor a response but an ongoing ____ process between the individual and the environment.
cards.back: Stress is neither a stimulus nor a response but an ongoing transactional process between the individual and the environment.
cards.quote: Stress is neither a stimulus nor a response but an ongoing transactional process between the individual and the environment.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The first approach views abnormal behaviour as a deviation from ____.
cards.back: The first approach views abnormal behaviour as a deviation from social norms.
cards.quote: The first approach views abnormal behaviour as a deviation from social norms.

source.section: Concepts of Abnormality and Psychological Disorders

reasons: review:'The first approach' has no antecedent on the card; 'deviation from ____' also fits 'the normal' or 'social expectations'. Name the context (normal vs abnormal behaviour).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Example: how may a competitive society and a cooperative society (such as India) differ on aggressive behaviour?
cards.back: Thus, a society whose culture values competition and assertiveness may accept aggressive behaviour, whereas one that emphasises cooperation and family values (such as in India) may consider aggressive behaviour as unacceptable or even abnormal.
cards.quote: Thus, a society whose culture values competition and assertiveness may accept aggressive behaviour, whereas one that emphasises cooperation and family values (such as in India) may consider aggressive behaviour as unacceptable or even abnormal.

source.section: Concepts of Abnormality and Psychological Disorders

reasons: review:Illustrative example (aggression in competitive vs cooperative society), not a testable definition or list; low exam value.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The second approach views abnormal behaviour as ____.
cards.back: The second approach views abnormal behaviour as maladaptive.
cards.quote: The second approach views abnormal behaviour as maladaptive.

source.section: Concepts of Abnormality and Psychological Disorders

reasons: review:'The second approach' has no antecedent; 'views abnormal behaviour as ____' also fits 'deviant' or 'a label'. Needs the approach named.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: the best criterion for determining the normality of behaviour is not whether society accepts it but whether it fosters the ____ of the individual and eventually of the group to which s/he belongs.

source.section: Concepts of Abnormality and Psychological Disorders

cards.front: According to this model, abnormal behaviour has a ____ basis.
cards.back: According to this model, abnormal behaviour has a biochemical or physiological basis.
cards.quote: According to this model, abnormal behaviour has a biochemical or physiological basis.
reasons: review:'According to this model' names no model on the card; 'biochemical or physiological' vs 'biological/genetic' is not fixed. Add 'biological model'.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Anxiety disorders have been linked to low activity of the neurotransmitter ____, schizophrenia to excess activity of ____, and depression to low activity of ____.
cards.back: Anxiety disorders have been linked to low activity of the neurotransmitter gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA), schizophrenia to excess activity of dopamine, and depression to low activity of serotonin.
cards.quote: Anxiety disorders have been linked to low activity of the neurotransmitter gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA), schizophrenia to excess activity of dopamine, and depression to low activity of serotonin.

blanks: bipolar and related disorders, schizophrenia, intellectual disability

cards.front: ____ cannot account for most mental disorders.
cards.back: biology alone cannot account for most mental disorders.
cards.quote: biology alone cannot account for most mental disorders.
reasons: review:'____ cannot account for most mental disorders' has no context; genetics, heredity or biochemistry also fit. Not one right fill.

cards.quote: This model states that both normal and abnormal behaviours are learned and psychological disorders are the result of learning maladaptive ways of behaving.

cards.front: People may hold assumptions and attitudes about themselves that are ____.
cards.back: People may hold assumptions and attitudes about themselves that are irrational and inaccurate.

cards.quote: people who are isolated and lack social support, i.e. strong and fulfilling interpersonal relationships in their lives are likely to become more depressed and remain depressed longer than those who have good friendships.

cards.front: Very often people who have been caught in a natural disaster (such as tsunami) or have been victims of bomb blasts by terrorists, or been in a serious accident or in a war-related situation, experience ____.

cards.quote: Very often people who have been caught in a natural disaster (such as tsunami) or have been victims of bomb blasts by terrorists, or been in a serious accident or in a war-related situation, experience post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

cards.quote: The purpose of the relationship is to help the client to solve the psychological problems being faced by her or him.
reasons: review:Blank 'solve' is a generic verb (solve/resolve/overcome all fit) and carries no marks; low exam value.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Psychotherapies aim at changing the ____ behaviours, decreasing the sense of personal distress, and helping the client to adapt better to her/his environment.
cards.back: Psychotherapies aim at changing the maladaptive behaviours, decreasing the sense of personal distress, and helping the client to adapt better to her/his environment.
cards.quote: Psychotherapies aim at changing the maladaptive behaviours, decreasing the sense of personal distress, and helping the client to adapt better to her/his environment.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: This is a ____, interpersonal, and dynamic relationship.
cards.back: This is a confidential, interpersonal, and dynamic relationship.
cards.quote: This is a confidential, interpersonal, and dynamic relationship.
cards.note: The therapist-client bond is described as confidential, interpersonal and dynamic.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The therapeutic alliance also requires that the therapist must keep strict ____ of the experiences, events, feelings or thoughts disclosed by the client.
cards.back: The therapeutic alliance also requires that the therapist must keep strict confidentiality of the experiences, events, feelings or thoughts disclosed by the client.
cards.quote: The therapeutic alliance also requires that the therapist must keep strict confidentiality of the experiences, events, feelings or thoughts disclosed by the client.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the 6 parameters on which psychotherapies are classified.
cards.back:
What is the cause, which has led to the problem?
How did the cause come into existence?
What is the chief method of treatment?
What is the nature of the therapeutic relationship between the client and the therapist?
What is the chief benefit to the client?
What is the duration of treatment?
cards.quote: The classification of psychotherapies is based on the following parameters:

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the 3 advantages of clinical formulation.
cards.back:
Understanding of the problem
Identification of the areas to be targetted for treatment in psychotherapy
Choice of techniques for treatment
cards.quote: The clinical formulation has the following advantages:

source.section: Steps in the Formulation of a Client's Problem

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The clinical formulation is an ____ process.
cards.back: The clinical formulation is an ongoing process.
cards.quote: The clinical formulation is an ongoing process.

source.section: Steps in the Formulation of a Client's Problem

reasons: review:'ongoing' has near synonyms (continuous/continuing) so a blank answer is not uniquely marked.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: It is not ____ to start psychotherapy without a clinical formulation.
cards.back: It is not advisable to start psychotherapy without a clinical formulation.
cards.quote: It is not advisable to start psychotherapy without a clinical formulation.

source.section: Steps in the Formulation of a Client's Problem

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: A young person started smoking during exam preparation and felt relief from anxiety. Name the antecedent and maintaining factors.
cards.back:
Antecedent factor: the anxiety-provoking situation. Maintaining factor: the feeling of relief.
Thus, anxiety-provoking situation becomes the causative or antecedent factor. The feeling of relief becomes the maintaining factor for him to continue smoking.
cards.quote: Thus, anxiety-provoking situation becomes the causative or antecedent factor. The feeling of relief becomes the maintaining factor for him to continue smoking.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The aim of the treatment is to extinguish or eliminate the faulty behaviours and ____ them with adaptive behaviour patterns.
cards.back: The aim of the treatment is to extinguish or eliminate the faulty behaviours and substitute them with adaptive behaviour patterns.
cards.quote: The aim of the treatment is to extinguish or eliminate the faulty behaviours and substitute them with adaptive behaviour patterns.
reasons: review:Blank 'substitute' has synonym 'replace'; generic verb, not mark-bearing.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: A child gives trouble in eating dinner. Which is the antecedent operation and which the consequent operation?
cards.back:
Antecedent operation: reduction of food at tea time. Consequent operation: praising the child for eating dinner.
The antecedent operation is the reduction of food at tea time and the consequent operation is praising the child for eating dinner.
cards.quote: The antecedent operation is the reduction of food at tea time and the consequent operation is praising the child for eating dinner.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: ____ are used to decrease the anxiety levels.
cards.back: Relaxation procedures are used to decrease the anxiety levels.
cards.quote: Relaxation procedures are used to decrease the anxiety levels.
reasons: review:Front '____ are used to decrease the anxiety levels' has no context; antianxiety drugs or other terms also fit.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: For instance, progressive muscular relaxation and ____ induce a state of relaxation.
cards.back: For instance, progressive muscular relaxation and meditation induce a state of relaxation.
cards.quote: For instance, progressive muscular relaxation and meditation induce a state of relaxation.
reasons: review:'For instance, progressive muscular relaxation and ____' admits yoga, deep breathing, biofeedback; only NCERT's 'meditation' is accepted.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In progressive muscular relaxation, the client is taught to ____ individual muscle groups in order to give the awareness of tenseness or muscular tension.
cards.back: In progressive muscular relaxation, the client is taught to contract individual muscle groups in order to give the awareness of tenseness or muscular tension.
cards.quote: In progressive muscular relaxation, the client is taught to contract individual muscle groups in order to give the awareness of tenseness or muscular tension.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Steps in systematic desensitisation, in order (first steps).
cards.back: The client is interviewed to elicit fear-provoking situations and together with the client, the therapist prepares a hierarchy of anxiety-provoking stimuli with the least anxiety-provoking stimuli at the bottom of the hierarchy. The therapist relaxes the client and asks the client to think about the least anxiety-provoking situation.
cards.quote: The client is interviewed to elicit fear-provoking situations and together with the client, the therapist prepares a hierarchy of anxiety-provoking stimuli with the least anxiety-provoking stimuli at the bottom of the hierarchy. The therapist relaxes the client and asks the client to think about the least anxiety-provoking situation.
reasons: review:Front says '(first steps)' and the back is a paragraph, not NCERT titled ordered steps, so the answer is vague and incomplete; systematic desensitisation procedure is a CUET staple and should be must.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: childhood experiences provided by the family and society develop ____ or systems, which include beliefs and action patterns in the individual.
cards.back: childhood experiences provided by the family and society develop core schemas or systems, which include beliefs and action patterns in the individual.
cards.quote: childhood experiences provided by the family and society develop core schemas or systems, which include beliefs and action patterns in the individual.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: These patterns of thought are called ____.
cards.back: These patterns of thought are called dysfunctional cognitive structures.
cards.quote: These patterns of thought are called dysfunctional cognitive structures.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The aim of the therapy is to achieve this ____ which, in turn, reduces anxiety and depression.
cards.back: The aim of the therapy is to achieve this cognitive restructuring which, in turn, reduces anxiety and depression.
cards.quote: The aim of the therapy is to achieve this cognitive restructuring which, in turn, reduces anxiety and depression.
reasons: review:'this ____' has no antecedent (which therapy, which aim?); front is ambiguous without the Beck context.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Unlike psycho-dynamic therapy, behaviour therapy is ____, i.e. the therapist shares her/his method with the client.
cards.back: Unlike psycho-dynamic therapy, behaviour therapy is open, i.e. the therapist shares her/his method with the client.
cards.quote: Unlike psycho-dynamic therapy, behaviour therapy is open, i.e. the therapist shares her/his method with the client.
reasons: review:NCERT sentence reads 'behaviour therapy is open' inside the Cognitive Therapy paragraph (likely misprint for cognitive therapy), and card id says cognitive; student will be misled. Needs owner call or removal.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: psychological distress arises from feelings of ____, ____, and an inability to find meaning and genuine fulfilment in life.
cards.back: psychological distress arises from feelings of loneliness, alienation, and an inability to find meaning and genuine fulfilment in life.
cards.quote: psychological distress arises from feelings of loneliness, alienation, and an inability to find meaning and genuine fulfilment in life.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The chief aim of the therapy is to expand the client's ____.
cards.back: The chief aim of the therapy is to expand the client's awareness.
cards.quote: The chief aim of the therapy is to expand the client's awareness.
reasons: review:'The chief aim of the therapy' names no therapy; gestalt (self-awareness) and others give different aims.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: there is a ____, which is the storehouse of love, aesthetic awareness, and values of life.
cards.back: there is a spiritual unconscious, which is the storehouse of love, aesthetic awareness, and values of life.
cards.quote: there is a spiritual unconscious, which is the storehouse of love, aesthetic awareness, and values of life.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Frankl emphasised the role of spiritual anxieties in leading to meaninglessness and hence it may be called an ____, i.e. neurotic anxiety of spiritual origin.
cards.back: Frankl emphasised the role of spiritual anxieties in leading to meaninglessness and hence it may be called an existential anxiety, i.e. neurotic anxiety of spiritual origin.
cards.quote: Frankl emphasised the role of spiritual anxieties in leading to meaninglessness and hence it may be called an existential anxiety, i.e. neurotic anxiety of spiritual origin.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The goal of logotherapy is to help the patients to find meaning and ____ in their life irrespective of their life circumstances.
cards.back: The goal of logotherapy is to help the patients to find meaning and responsibility in their life irrespective of their life circumstances.
cards.quote: The goal of logotherapy is to help the patients to find meaning and responsibility in their life irrespective of their life circumstances.
reasons: review:'find meaning and ____' - 'purpose' fits equally; only 'responsibility' is NCERT's.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In client-centred therapy, what does the therapist show (empathy and unconditional positive regard)?
cards.back: The therapist shows empathy, i.e. understanding the client's experience as if it were her/his own, is warm and has unconditional positive regard, i.e. total acceptance of the client as s/he is.
cards.quote: The therapist shows empathy, i.e. understanding the client's experience as if it were her/his own, is warm and has unconditional positive regard, i.e. total acceptance of the client as s/he is.
reasons: review:Front gives away the answer in brackets (empathy and unconditional positive regard) and duplicates the separate empathy and UPR cards.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Empathy sets up an ____ between the therapist and the client.
cards.back: Empathy sets up an emotional resonance between the therapist and the client.
cards.quote: Empathy sets up an emotional resonance between the therapist and the client.
reasons: review:'Empathy sets up an ____' - emotional bond/connection/rapport also fit; 'emotional resonance' is not uniquely derivable.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The reflection is achieved by ____ the statements of the client, i.e. seeking simple clarifications to enhance the meaning of the client's statements.
cards.back: The reflection is achieved by rephrasing the statements of the client, i.e. seeking simple clarifications to enhance the meaning of the client's statements.
cards.quote: The reflection is achieved by rephrasing the statements of the client, i.e. seeking simple clarifications to enhance the meaning of the client's statements.
reasons: review:Blank 'rephrasing' has synonyms (restating/repeating/paraphrasing); not uniquely answerable.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In essence, this therapy helps a client to become her/his ____ with the therapist working as a facilitator.
cards.back: In essence, this therapy helps a client to become her/his real self with the therapist working as a facilitator.
cards.quote: In essence, this therapy helps a client to become her/his real self with the therapist working as a facilitator.
reasons: review:'this therapy' is not identified in front (client-centred), so many humanistic goals could fill the blank.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The therapist does this by encouraging the client to ____ fantasies about feelings and conflicts.
cards.back: The therapist does this by encouraging the client to act out fantasies about feelings and conflicts.
cards.quote: The therapist does this by encouraging the client to act out fantasies about feelings and conflicts.
reasons: review:'The therapist does this by...' has no antecedent; 'act out' vs 'enact/express' not unique.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the factors that contribute to healing in psychotherapy.
cards.back:
A major factor in the healing is the techniques adopted by the therapist and the implementation of the same with the patient/client.
The therapeutic alliance, which is formed between the therapist and the patient/client, has healing properties
This process of emotional unburdening is known as catharsis, and it has healing properties.
There are several non-specific factors associated with psychotherapy.
cards.quote: There are several factors which contribute to the healing process. Some of these factors are as follows : 1. A major factor in the healing is the techniques adopted by the therapist and the implementation of the same with the patient/client.

source.section: Factors Contributing to Healing in Psychotherapy

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: This process of emotional unburdening is known as ____, and it has healing properties.
cards.back: This process of emotional unburdening is known as catharsis, and it has healing properties.
cards.quote: This process of emotional unburdening is known as catharsis, and it has healing properties.

source.section: Factors Contributing to Healing in Psychotherapy

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: SKY has been used as a public health intervention technique to alleviate PTSD in survivors of ____.
cards.back: SKY has been used as a public health intervention technique to alleviate PTSD in survivors of mass disasters.
cards.quote: SKY has been used as a public health intervention technique to alleviate PTSD in survivors of mass disasters.
reasons: review:Trivia (survivors of 'mass disasters'); low CUET value.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: However, in the case of severe mental disorders such as ____, reduction of symptoms may not be associated with an improvement in the quality of life.
cards.back: However, in the case of severe mental disorders such as schizophrenia, reduction of symptoms may not be associated with an improvement in the quality of life.
cards.quote: However, in the case of severe mental disorders such as schizophrenia, reduction of symptoms may not be associated with an improvement in the quality of life.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The aim of rehabilitation is to ____ the patient to become a productive member of society to the extent possible.
cards.back: The aim of rehabilitation is to empower the patient to become a productive member of society to the extent possible.
cards.quote: The aim of rehabilitation is to empower the patient to become a productive member of society to the extent possible.
reasons: review:Blank 'empower' has synonyms (enable/help); not uniquely answerable.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: It is accompanied by an ____ component, and a ____ in a particular way with regard to the attitude object.
cards.back: It is accompanied by an emotional component, and a tendency to act in a particular way with regard to the attitude object.
cards.quote: It is accompanied by an emotional component, and a tendency to act in a particular way with regard to the attitude object.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: They are part of ____, along with an emotional component, and cannot be observed from outside.
cards.back: They are part of cognition, along with an emotional component, and cannot be observed from outside.
cards.quote: They are part of cognition, along with an emotional component, and cannot be observed from outside.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: On the nuclear research scale, how does a rating of 1 compare with a rating of 5 on extremeness?
cards.back: Taking the nuclear research example given above, a rating of 1 is as extreme as a rating of 5 : they are only in the opposite directions (valence).
cards.quote: Taking the nuclear research example given above, a rating of 1 is as extreme as a rating of 5 : they are only in the opposite directions (valence).
reasons: review:Illustration only: the 1-5 nuclear-research scale is not shown on the card and the back says 'given above'; the concept is already carried by the extremeness definition.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the processes of attitude formation (learning of attitudes).
cards.back:
Learning attitudes by association
Learning attitudes by being rewarded or punished
Learning attitudes through modelling (observing others)
Learning attitudes through group or cultural norms
Learning through exposure to information
cards.quote: The processes and conditions of learning may be different, resulting in varying attitudes among people.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the factors that influence attitude formation.
cards.back:
Family and School Environment
Reference Groups
Personal Experiences
Media-related Influences
cards.quote: The following factors provide the context for the learning of attitudes through the processes described above.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: An army driver, sole survivor of a mission, becomes a community leader. Which factor in attitude formation?
cards.back:
Personal experiences
Through a purely personal experience this individual evolved a strong positive attitude towards community upliftment.
cards.quote: Through a purely personal experience this individual evolved a strong positive attitude towards community upliftment.
reasons: review:Case-story filler (army driver anecdote); the factor 'Personal experiences' is already covered by the list card.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: These sources first strengthen the ____ components of attitudes, and subsequently may also affect the ____ component.
cards.back: These sources first strengthen the cognitive and affective components of attitudes, and subsequently may also affect the behavioural component.
cards.quote: These sources first strengthen the cognitive and affective components of attitudes, and subsequently may also affect the behavioural component.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What valence would a neutral attitude have?
cards.back: A neutral attitude would have neither positive nor negative valence.
cards.quote: A neutral attitude would have neither positive nor negative valence.
reasons: review:Circular trivia: a neutral attitude has neither positive nor negative valence follows from the word neutral; not a mark-carrying fact.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the three major concepts of the process of attitude change.
cards.back:
The concept of balance
The concept of cognitive dissonance
The two-step concept
cards.quote: Three major concepts that draw attention to some important processes in attitude change are described below :

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In Box 6.2, why did the $ 1 students change their attitude towards the experiment?
cards.back: The explanation was : the $ 1 students changed their attitude towards the experiment because they experienced cognitive dissonance.
cards.quote: The explanation was : the $ 1 students changed their attitude towards the experiment because they experienced cognitive dissonance.
reasons: review:Front depends on Box 6.2 (what the experiment was, who the '$1 students' are) which the card does not state; add the experiment to the front.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In Box 6.2, why did the $ 20 group not change its attitude?
cards.back: The $ 20 group did not experience cognitive dissonance. So, they did not change their attitude towards the experiment, and rated it as very boring.
cards.quote: The $ 20 group did not experience cognitive dissonance. So, they did not change their attitude towards the experiment, and rated it as very boring.
reasons: review:Front depends on Box 6.2 (the '$20 group' and the experiment are not described on the card); add the context to the front.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Steps in Mohsin’s two-step concept of attitude change, in order.
cards.back:
In the first step, the target of change identifies with the source.
In the second step, the source herself/himself shows an attitude change, by actually changing her/him behaviour towards the attitude object.
cards.quote: In the first step, the target of change identifies with the source.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the major factors that influence attitude change.
cards.back:
Characteristics of the existing attitude
Source characteristics
Message characteristics
Target characteristics
cards.quote: However, most of them agree upon the following major factors that influence attitude change :

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: When is there consistency between attitudes and behaviour?
cards.back:
the attitude is strong, and occupies a central place in the attitude system
the person is aware of her/his attitude
there is very little or no external pressure for the person to behave in a particular way
the person’s behaviour is not being watched or evaluated by others
the person thinks that the behaviour would have a positive consequence, and therefore, intends to engage in that behaviour
cards.quote: Psychologists have found that there would be consistency between attitudes and behaviour when :

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In the $ 1 group of Box 6.2, what did the students conclude on the basis of their behaviour?
cards.back: That is, on the basis of their behaviour (telling others that the experiment was interesting, for only a small amount of money), they concluded that their attitude towards the experiment was positive
cards.quote: That is, on the basis of their behaviour (telling others that the experiment was interesting, for only a small amount of money), they concluded that their attitude towards the experiment was positive
reasons: review:Front depends on Box 6.2 (the experiment is not described) and the back starts 'That is,' with no antecedent and drops the sentence end; answer is vague without context.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The cognitive component of prejudice is frequently accompanied by dislike or hatred, the ____ component.
cards.back: The cognitive component of prejudice is frequently accompanied by dislike or hatred, the affective component.
cards.quote: The cognitive component of prejudice is frequently accompanied by dislike or hatred, the affective component.
reasons: review:'emotional' fits the blank as well as 'affective' (NCERT itself calls it 'affective (emotional)'); two right fills.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the sources of prejudice.
cards.back:
Learning
A strong social identity and ingroup bias
Scapegoating
Kernel of truth concept
Self-fulfilling prophecy
cards.quote: Social psychologists have shown that prejudice has one or more of the following sources :

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Scapegoating is a group-based way of expressing ____, and it often results in negative attitudes or prejudice against the weaker group.
cards.back: Scapegoating is a group-based way of expressing frustration, and it often results in negative attitudes or prejudice against the weaker group.
cards.quote: Scapegoating is a group-based way of expressing frustration, and it often results in negative attitudes or prejudice against the weaker group.
reasons: review:Alternatives such as anger, hostility or aggression also fit 'a group-based way of expressing ____'; only the NCERT word 'frustration' is accepted.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Strategies for handling prejudice are effective if they aim at which four things?
cards.back:
minimising opportunities for learning prejudices
changing such attitudes
de-emphasising a narrow social identity based on the ingroup
discouraging the tendency towards self-fulfilling prophecy among the victims of prejudice
cards.quote: Thus, the strategies for handling prejudice would be effective if they aim at :

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the ways of accomplishing the goals of handling prejudice.
cards.back:
Education and information dissemination
Increasing intergroup contact
Highlighting individual identity rather than group identity
cards.quote: These goals can be accomplished through :

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Intergroup contact strategies succeed only if which three conditions hold?
cards.back:
the two groups meet in a cooperative rather than competitive context
close interactions between the groups helps them to know each other better
the two groups are not different in power or status
cards.quote: However, these strategies are successful only if :

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the salient characteristics of groups.
cards.back:
A social unit consisting of two or more individuals who perceive themselves as belonging to the group.
A collection of individuals who have common motives and goals.
A collection of individuals who are interdependent, i.e. what one is doing may have consequences for others.
Individuals who are trying to satisfy a need through their joint association also influence each other.
A gathering of individuals who interact with one another either directly or indirectly.
A collection of individuals whose interactions are structured by a set of roles and norms.
cards.quote: Groups have the following salient characteristics :

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: ____, roles, status, and ____ are the main characteristics of groups.
cards.back: Mutual interdependence, roles, status, and expectations are the main characteristics of groups.
cards.quote: Mutual interdependence, roles, status, and expectations are the main characteristics of groups.
reasons: review:Ambiguous: Second blank has other fits (norms, cohesiveness); 'expectations' is not forced by the line. Importance: Summary point; spec makes summary points must.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: There is neither any ____ nor feeling of ____ in a crowd.
cards.back: There is neither any structure nor feeling of belongingness in a crowd.
cards.quote: There is neither any structure nor feeling of belongingness in a crowd.
reasons: review:Ambiguous: First blank 'structure' has close synonyms (organisation); two blanks.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Behaviour of people in crowds is ____ and there is no interdependence among members.
cards.back: Behaviour of people in crowds is irrational and there is no interdependence among members.
cards.quote: Behaviour of people in crowds is irrational and there is no interdependence among members.
reasons: review:Ambiguous: 'irrational' has plausible alternatives (impulsive, unpredictable); not a forced fill.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Audiences are generally ____ but sometimes they go into a frenzy and become ____.
cards.back: Audiences are generally passive but sometimes they go into a frenzy and become mobs.
cards.quote: Audiences are generally passive but sometimes they go into a frenzy and become mobs.
reasons: review:Ambiguous: 'passive' has equal fits (calm, quiet, peaceful); not a forced fill.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Mob behaviour is characterised by ____ of thought and behaviour as well as ____.
cards.back: Mob behaviour is characterised by homogeneity of thought and behaviour as well as impulsivity.
cards.quote: Mob behaviour is characterised by homogeneity of thought and behaviour as well as impulsivity.
reasons: review:Ambiguous: Both blanks have synonyms (uniformity; emotionality/irrationality); not a forced fill.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the reasons why people join groups.
cards.back:
Security: When we are alone, we feel insecure.
Status: When we are members of a group that is perceived to be important by others, we feel recognised and experience a sense of power.
Self-esteem: Groups provide feelings of self-worth and establish a positive social identity.
Satisfaction of one’s psychological and social needs: Groups satisfy one’s social and psychological needs such as sense of belongingness, giving and receiving attention, love, and power through a group.
Goal achievement: Groups help in achieving such goals which cannot be attained individually.
Provide knowledge and information: Group membership provides knowledge and information and thus broadens our view.
cards.quote: People join groups because these groups satisfy a range of needs.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Another explanation given by psychologists is that when we meet similar people, they reinforce and ____ our opinions and values
cards.back: Another explanation given by psychologists is that when we meet similar people, they reinforce and validate our opinions and values
cards.quote: Another explanation given by psychologists is that when we meet similar people, they reinforce and validate our opinions and values
reasons: review:Ambiguous: 'reinforce and ____' fits strengthen/support/confirm equally; 'validate' is not forced.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: When people have common ____ or goals, they get together and form a group which may facilitate their goal attainment.
cards.back: When people have common motives or goals, they get together and form a group which may facilitate their goal attainment.
cards.quote: When people have common motives or goals, they get together and form a group which may facilitate their goal attainment.
reasons: review:Ambiguous: 'motives' has equal fits (aims, interests, objectives) before 'or goals'.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: When this stage is complete, some sort of ____ of leadership in the group develops and a clear vision as to how to achieve the group goal.
cards.back: When this stage is complete, some sort of hierarchy of leadership in the group develops and a clear vision as to how to achieve the group goal.
cards.quote: When this stage is complete, some sort of hierarchy of leadership in the group develops and a clear vision as to how to achieve the group goal.
reasons: review:Ambiguous: 'this stage' has no antecedent in the front (storming is never named), so the card cannot be answered; 'hierarchy' also has synonyms (structure).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the four important elements of group structure.
cards.back:
Roles
Norms
Status
Cohesiveness
cards.quote: Four important elements of group structure are :

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Cohesiveness refers to the ____ or ‘we feeling’ or a sense of belongingness to the group.
cards.back: Cohesiveness refers to the team spirit or ‘we feeling’ or a sense of belongingness to the group.
cards.quote: Cohesiveness refers to the team spirit or ‘we feeling’ or a sense of belongingness to the group.
reasons: review:Ambiguous: 'team spirit' competes with 'togetherness' (given in the definition sentence); two-word blank.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: As the group becomes more cohesive, group members start to think, feel and act as a ____, and less like isolated individuals.
cards.back: As the group becomes more cohesive, group members start to think, feel and act as a social unit, and less like isolated individuals.
cards.quote: As the group becomes more cohesive, group members start to think, feel and act as a social unit, and less like isolated individuals.
reasons: review:Ambiguous: 'act as a ____' fits group/unit/team equally; 'social unit' not forced.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Groupthink is likely to occur in socially ____, cohesive groups that are ____ from outsiders
cards.back: Groupthink is likely to occur in socially homogenous, cohesive groups that are isolated from outsiders
cards.quote: Groupthink is likely to occur in socially homogenous, cohesive groups that are isolated from outsiders
reasons: review:Ambiguous: Both blanks have close synonyms (similar/uniform; cut off/separated).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Primary groups are central to individual’s functioning and have a very major role in developing ____ and ____ of the individual
cards.back: Primary groups are central to individual’s functioning and have a very major role in developing values and ideals of the individual
cards.quote: Primary groups are central to individual’s functioning and have a very major role in developing values and ideals of the individual
reasons: review:Ambiguous: Blanks 'values and ideals' have plausible alternatives (beliefs, attitudes, personality).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In contrast, secondary groups are those where relationships among members are more ____, ____, and less frequent.
cards.back: In contrast, secondary groups are those where relationships among members are more impersonal, indirect, and less frequent.
cards.quote: In contrast, secondary groups are those where relationships among members are more impersonal, indirect, and less frequent.

cards.front: Name the explanations offered for why social loafing occurs.
cards.back:
Group members feel less responsible for the overall task being performed and therefore exert less effort.
Motivation of members decreases because they realise that their contributions will not be evaluated on individual basis.
The performance of the group is not to be compared with other groups.
There is an improper coordination (or no coordination) among members.
Belonging to the same group is not important for members.

cards.front: Name the ways in which social loafing may be reduced.
cards.back:
Making the efforts of each person identifiable.
Increasing the pressure to work hard (making group members committed to successful task performance).
Increasing the apparent importance or value of a task.
Making people feel that their individual contribution is important.
Strengthening group cohesiveness which increases the motivation for successful group outcome.

In the company of like-minded people, you are likely to hear newer arguments favouring your viewpoints.
